title: Can you break the sealed contract via reflection or bytecode manipulation?
shortTitle: Can you break the sealed contract via reflection or bytecode manipulation?

s1_definition.profdef: The sealed contract is enforced primarily by the compiler and, crucially, re-verified by the JVM at class-load and link time using the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute. You cannot trick normal reflection into creating an unlisted subclass, because defining a class that extends a sealed type without being in its permits list throws an `IncompatibleClassChangeError` at load time. However, the sealed contract is a classfile-level integrity rule, not a security boundary: with raw bytecode manipulation you can hand-craft or rewrite class files to remove or alter the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute, and if you can load those modified classes, the JVM will accept them. So you "break" it only by forging the verified metadata, not through legitimate reflection.
s1_definition.analogy: The sealed permits list is like a vault's approved-signatory list that the security system checks every time someone tries to enter. If Rajesh is not on the list, the guard turns him away at load time — there is no polite reflection trick to sneak him in. But the sealed contract is an integrity seal, not an unbreakable vault door: if a malicious insider literally rewrites the official signatory document (edits the raw bytecode) and gets that forged document accepted into the system, the guard will honor the forged list. The seal protects against accidents and honest mistakes, not against someone who controls and rewrites the class files themselves.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reflection cannot break sealing because the JVM re-checks the permits list at load time, but raw bytecode edits can forge that metadata, so sealing is an integrity guarantee, not a security sandbox.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The sealed contract is enforced primarily by the compiler and, crucially, re-verified by the JVM at class-load and link time using the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute. You cannot trick normal reflection into creating an unlisted subclass, because defining a class that extends a sealed type without being in its permits list throws an `IncompatibleClassChangeError` at load time. However, the sealed contract is a classfile-level integrity rule, not a security boundary: with raw bytecode manipulation you can hand-craft or rewrite class files to remove or alter the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute, and if you can load those modified classes, the JVM will accept them. So you "break" it only by forging the verified metadata, not through legitimate reflection.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The sealed permits list is like a vault's approved-signatory list that the security system checks every time someone tries to enter. If Rajesh is not on the list, the guard turns him away at load time — there is no polite reflection trick to sneak him in. But the sealed contract is an integrity seal, not an unbreakable vault door: if a malicious insider literally rewrites the official signatory document (edits the raw bytecode) and gets that forged document accepted into the system, the guard will honor the forged list. The seal protects against accidents and honest mistakes, not against someone who controls and rewrites the class files themselves.

**One line to remember:** Reflection cannot break sealing because the JVM re-checks the permits list at load time, but raw bytecode edits can forge that metadata, so sealing is an integrity guarantee, not a security sandbox.

sections.s2_technical:
When you compile a sealed class, the compiler writes a `PermittedSubclasses` attribute listing the allowed subtypes, and each subtype must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. This is not only a compile-time check. The JVM verifier, during class loading and linking, checks that any class declaring a sealed type as its direct superclass or superinterface actually appears in that superclass's permitted list, and that both live in the same module (or same package for the unnamed module). If the check fails, loading throws `IncompatibleClassChangeError`. That is why you cannot simply use `Class.forName` plus a dynamically defined subclass to break in — the verifier stops you.

Reflection, specifically, does not give you a backdoor. `Proxy.newProxyInstance` cannot implement a sealed interface, and even if you use a library like ByteBuddy or ASM to generate a subclass at runtime, the generated class still has to pass the same load-time permitted-subclasses verification, so it fails unless the sealed parent lists it. For example, attempting to generate `class RogueProduct extends SavingsProduct` and load it will throw at definition time if `SavingsProduct` is `final` (which records are) or if `RogueProduct` is not permitted.

Bytecode manipulation is the real escape hatch, and understanding why matters at a senior level. The sealed guarantee is encoded entirely in the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute of the parent classfile. If an attacker can edit that classfile to add a name, or strip the attribute entirely, and then arrange for the JVM to load the tampered classfile instead of the real one, the verifier will happily accept the forged metadata because it only checks consistency against whatever attribute is present. This means sealing is an integrity constraint that holds as long as the classfiles are trustworthy. The senior takeaway is that sealing is for API design and compiler-enforced exhaustiveness, not for defending against an adversary who controls your class files or classloaders. Genuine security against tampered bytecode comes from other layers: code signing and jar signature verification, running with integrity-protected deployment artifacts, module strong encapsulation, and not loading untrusted classes. In a banking deployment I rely on signed artifacts and immutable containers so the classfiles the JVM loads cannot be the forged ones.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India seals its `AccountProduct` hierarchy so only three approved products exist. A developer wonders whether a clever reflection trick could smuggle in a fourth, unapproved product at runtime. The bank needs to demonstrate that the JVM itself blocks this. This is exactly how load-time sealed verification works — the JVM re-checks the permits list and refuses an unlisted subclass.

Problem 2 — The security team must understand the real threat model: if an attacker can replace the bank's class files with hand-edited bytecode, the seal can be forged. The bank therefore relies on signed artifacts, not on sealing, for tamper protection. This is exactly why sealing is an integrity feature, not a security boundary.

The demo seals `AccountProduct`, attempts to runtime-generate a rogue subclass (via a small simulated attempt that catches the resulting error), and logs why it fails, then documents in comments how bytecode forging would bypass it and what real defense (signed jars) looks like. Classes and steps: `AccountProduct` (sealed), `SavingsProduct`/`CurrentProduct`/`FixedDepositProduct` (permitted records), `SealBreakAttempt` (tries and fails, logs the error), and `BankDemo` (main).

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.integrity.BankDemo

# Verify a jar is signed (real tamper defense):
jarsigner -verify -verbose target/sealed-integrity-demo-1.0.0.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sealed `AccountProduct` with three permitted records, and a runtime attempt to create a rogue fourth product.

Step 1 — At startup the JVM has already loaded `AccountProduct` and verified its `PermittedSubclasses` attribute lists exactly `SavingsProduct`, `CurrentProduct`, and `FixedDepositProduct`.

Step 2 — `BankDemo` prints the permitted set, confirming the closed list the verifier will enforce.

Step 3 — `SealBreakAttempt.tryReflectiveSubclass` tries to bring an unlisted subclass into existence. The JVM verifier rejects it because the class is not in the permits list and the records are final, producing `IncompatibleClassChangeError`, which we log at SEVERE with the full stack trace.

Step 4 — The demo then documents that the only way to actually defeat the seal is to forge the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute via bytecode manipulation and load the tampered classfile, and that real protection is signed artifacts, logged as a WARNING so the threat model is explicit.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Sealed permitted set: [class ...SavingsProduct, class ...CurrentProduct, class ...FixedDepositProduct]
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [SEVERE] Reflective seal-break BLOCKED by JVM verifier
java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class RogueProduct cannot inherit from sealed/final AccountProduct member ...
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [WARNING] Sealing is an INTEGRITY guarantee, not a security sandbox. Tamper protection comes from signed artifacts, not from sealed.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  App tries to create subclass of sealed AccountProduct
    │
    ├─ via REFLECTION / ByteBuddy / ASM (honest runtime)
    │     ▼
    │   JVM Verifier (load/link time)
    │     │ check: is class in PermittedSubclasses? is parent final?
    │     ▼
    │   NOT permitted → IncompatibleClassChangeError  ✗ BLOCKED
    │
    └─ via BYTECODE FORGERY (rewrite the parent classfile)
          ▼
        edit PermittedSubclasses attribute (add name / delete attr)
          ▼
        load TAMPERED AccountProduct.class
          ▼
        Verifier checks consistency vs FORGED attribute → accepted  ✗ SEAL FORGED
          ▼
        Real defense: signed jars, immutable images, no untrusted classloaders
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
You cannot break the sealed contract through legitimate reflection, because sealing is not only a compile-time rule, it is re-verified by the JVM at class-load and link time using the permitted-subclasses attribute. If any class tries to extend or implement a sealed type without being on its permits list, or tries to subclass one of its final record members, the verifier throws IncompatibleClassChangeError at load time. Reflection APIs, dynamic proxies, and runtime bytecode generators all still have to pass that same verification, so none of them give you a backdoor into the closed set.

The honest answer, though, is that sealing is an integrity guarantee, not a security boundary. The entire guarantee lives in the permitted-subclasses attribute of the parent class file. If an attacker can rewrite that class file with a tool like ASM to add a rogue name or strip the attribute, and then get the JVM to load the tampered class file, the verifier will accept the forged metadata because it only checks consistency against whatever attribute is present. So raw bytecode manipulation can forge the seal in a way that reflection never can.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this distinction drives real decisions. I seal the account-product hierarchy to get compiler-enforced exhaustiveness and a clean, closed API, and I rely on the JVM verifier to stop any accidental or reflective attempt to introduce an unapproved product. But I never treat sealing as my defense against a malicious party who controls the deployment. For that I rely on signed jars verified at load time, immutable and signed container images, module strong encapsulation, and a strict policy of never loading untrusted classes.

So in an interview I phrase it precisely: reflection cannot break sealing because the JVM checks the permits list at load time, but bytecode forgery can, because the guarantee is only as trustworthy as the class files the JVM loads. That is why I pair sealing with artifact signing and immutable deployments to get both the design benefit and genuine tamper resistance.
